newsitem.title: UK: Japanese thirst for US bonds not quenched-analysts.
newsitem.headline: Japanese thirst for US bonds not quenched-analysts.

text.p: By Jacqueline Thorpe,
Speculation that Japanese investors will lose their thirst for U.S. Treasuries lashed bond markets on Wednesday but analysts said the concerns were overplayed.
While temporary dollar weakness may cause some investors to pause for breath as the year ends, Japanese interest in U.S. bonds boils down to one thing -- the search for yield.
The search will continue as long as Japanese government bonds continue to offer meagre yields compared with other government bonds, analysts said.

"The long-term trend is that Japanese investors will continue to build up their holdings overseas because they need the return," Julian Jessop, economist at Nikko Europe in London said. "The return on JGBs (Japanese government bonds) is under 2.5 percent and that's not enough."
Treasuries, still bruised by their pummelling last week amid concerns about the speculative nature of the recent rally, lurched lower again in Asian and European trading on Wednesday.

The decline was partly due to renewed speculation that Japanese investors would curtail buying amid the trading turbulence, year-end position squaring and concerns that recent dollar strength was set to wane.

Data released earlier on Wednesday showing a 31.3 percent rise in Japan's trade surplus with the United States in October heightened the unease. The dollar was quoted at 112.74 yen at 1430 GMT compared with 113.27 in Europe late on Tuesday.

Japanese investors have profited handsomely this year by borrowing in yen at low interest rates, then switching into dollars to buy U.S. debt. Ten-year Treasuries yield around 6.1 percent compared with 2.5 percent for equivalent Japanese bonds.
The flow of funds has been non-stop, analysts said.

"All year long, official and unofficial," said Charles Quigley, bond salesman at Chase in London. "Not just outright buying of Treasuries securities but also the use of derivatives, and bullish trades in the swap markets."
Kirit Shah, chief market strategist at Sanwa International in London, added the buying has not only been from the Bank of Japan this year, seen as the main player in 1995.
"This year we've seen a more diversified pool -- insurance companies, financial institutions and pension funds," he said. "The strength of the dollar has brought in many other players."

Figures from the Ministry of Finance in Japan on Wednesday confirmed the buying. Net purchases of U.S. bonds by Japanese investors increased sharply in October to 1.0 trillion yen ($8.8 billion) from 249.6 billion yen in Septebmer.
Purchases of foreign bonds in total increased to 1.7 trillion yen from 446.1 billion yen in September.
Keith Edmonds, chief analyst at IBJ in London, said that brought buying of foreign bonds in the year to date to around 7.7 trillion yen compared with 8.5 trillion in all of 1996.

The October buying spree should safisfy Japanese investors for now, analysts said, leading to a temporary halt in the flow of funds just as the yen traditionally strengthens against the dollar into the end of the year.
"It's not so much they are liquidating their holdings, they've reached their desired levels. The flows into the market are set to diminish but there is not going to be a net outflow," Edmonds said.
Jessop at Nikko agreed.
"There's not a big incentive to take an additional risk this close to the end of the fiscal year," he said.

He said the dollar may weaken down to around 105 yen in the next three months or so but the overall trend is not too gloomy, with the dollar expected to rebound from there up to around 115-120 yen into next year, he said.
-- International Bonds Unit +44 171 542 6176 ($1=112.7 Yen)
